claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A multi-fidelity, physics-informed surrogate using microstructural descriptors can accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate will require substantially less computation than prior prediction methods.
Local compositional variance and defect density can serve as rapidly obtained, low-cost microstructural descriptors.
The surrogate will fuse low-fidelity microstructural descriptors with selected finite-element or first-principles outputs and use physics-informed machine learning for calibration.
The multilevel chemical fluctuations, local compositional variability, and defect distributions modulate local mechanical response.
Chemical heterogeneity is correlated with mechanical performance.
Embedding fracture-mechanics scaling laws and using experimental descriptors to guide simulation outputs will reduce prediction uncertainty.
Embedding physics constraints and experimental descriptors will reduce computational runtime relative to conventional full-scale simulations.
Prediction error for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness will decrease by approximately 20–30%.
Computational cost will decrease by nearly 50% relative to the stated prior methods.
Extensive CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and conventional machine-learning models have high computational demands.
The approach may become unreliable if the hierarchical microstructure evolves substantially during testing, including through phase changes or degradation at high temperature or extreme strain rate.
The approach may become unreliable when its low-cost descriptors omit microstructural features that critically affect mechanical performance.
The magnitude of the accuracy and runtime gains depends on descriptor quality and the availability of calibrated high-fidelity data.
The model is to be evaluated against standardized tensile and fracture measurements of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness on HfNbTiVAl10 samples.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% and computational cost by approximately 50% relative to high-fidelity methods is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes or anticipates unreliability when the microstructure changes substantially, but the falsification rule treats discrepancies correlated with unforeseen microstructural changes as falsification. A result attributed to an excluded condition should not simultaneously be decisive evidence against the in-boundary hypothesis.
